claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a high-temperature disordered solid solution.
Temperature-dependent short-range ordering develops in HfNbTaTiZr during processing.
Short-range ordering creates nanoscale regions having different thermal expansion coefficients.
Short-range ordering produces local lattice-parameter variations.
Local thermal-expansion mismatch generates internal residual stresses.
The internal residual stresses interact with dislocations and thereby modify creep and plastic deformation.
Short-range-order-induced residual stresses modify the alloy's elastic-modulus behavior.
Short-range-order-induced residual stresses govern aging hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
Rapid quenching from high temperature retains a predominantly disordered HfNbTaTiZr state with little short-range order.
Slow cooling permits more short-range order to develop than rapid quenching.
Atom-probe tomography or high-resolution TEM can quantitatively distinguish the proposed short-range-order distributions.
Slow-cooled samples will show greater temperature-dependent elastic-modulus variability than rapidly quenched samples over 293–1100 K.
Slow-cooled samples will have lower creep rates at 1250 °C than rapidly quenched samples under the same load.
Slow-cooled and rapidly quenched samples will have measurably different thermal expansion coefficients.
The proposed effect is relevant only when sufficient short-range order develops under suitable cooling rates or aging durations.
The comparison will evaluate creep at about 1250 °C, elastic modulus from 293 to 1100 K, and aging-induced hardness changes after treatments at 600–800 °C.
The magnitude of the short-range-order contribution may be modest and confounded by other microstructural factors.
